answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Benefits:
- Measurable Impact and Defensible Claims. Consequential accounting allows companies to demonstrate measurable, real-world climate benefits.
- Long-term Planning. Consequential accounting aligns corporate actions with national decarbonization targets and offers more consistency between private and public efforts.
- Capital Efficiency and Innovation. By linking emissions outcomes to time and location, companies can compare interventions by cost per tonne of CO2 avoided and focus investment on technologies/solutions that maximize system value.

Challenges:
- Cost. High-quality consequential analysis is data- and expertise-intensive, which raises costs for users, especially outside well-modelled markets. To avoid “pricing out” organizations that would otherwise voluntarily participate in renewable/clean energy purchases and GHG accounting/disclosure, the data for avoided emissions must be widely available.

- Reporting Complexity. If consequential impacts are calculated annually, emission accounting will require updated marginal emission rates as the grid (and models) evolve. The additional complexity may discourage firms from action. This challenge is avoided if the “avoided emissions” (impact) is calculated once at the time of contract/COD and applied consistently over the contract term.

- Eroding Benefit. If consequential impacts are calculated annually, the impact of a purchase/investment erodes as the grid decarbonizes. Long-term commitments needed to finance new renewable energy projects may be difficult for many firms. This challenge is avoided, if the “avoided emissions” (impact) is calculated once at the time of contract/COD and firms have confidence in the emission benefit over the contract term.
- Standardization and Governance. Without a standard and common approach to modelling “avoided emissions” (impact) of a purchase/investment, organizations may be reluctant to enter long-term agreements or make significant investments in regions where the accounting methodology is less certain or less viable.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Regulatory test - Required
Renewable purchases that are required by law or market design are not to be considered “additional.” However, the regulatory test is not comprehensive, as the voluntary purchase of energy attribute certificates from existing/merchant generators does not provide the financial commitments necessary to bring new generation to market.
Timing test - Required
Simple, objective, and politically neutral. Ensures operational projects are not counted as newly additional.
Contractual / tenor test - Optional
Term length does not necessarily define “additionality.” For example, firms that install solar generation through capital investments do not have a term as those installations are purchased outright. These systems would not exist without the firms’ commitment, but they also do not carry an applicable term length. Further, the purchase of a 5 or 10-year contract for EACs from an existing clean energy asset does not offer “additionality,” as that asset is already producing energy and in the current generation stack.
Positive list – Optional, highly feasible.
Positive lists are already used in formats like RE100, so for many buyers it is straightforward to show that a project falls into an approved category. However, because not all regions or actors are covered by existing lists, and lists can become outdated as markets evolve, it is better to treat them as an easy optional route to demonstrate additionality rather than a universal requirement.
Financial, barrier, common practice, and performance standards – Optional and feasible in many instances. Any purchase/investment made prior to a project’s financial close can be considered “additional,” as it provides the revenue certainty to secure the internal or third-party financial commitments necessary to build the project.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
Common practice/performance standard, both require market data and careful boundary setting but are widely used in carbon standards and can be implemented where robust statistics exist, but not in all markets.

Financial and barrier tests demand granular project data, developer cooperation, and expert judgement, which can be costly and inconsistent across regions.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: The definition of additionality should be consistent across markets. However, the method to demonstrate additionality may differ based on available information. A hierarchy of testing methods may be appropriate to allow organizations that support additional projects to demonstrate the additionality in circumstances where data/documentation may not be as readily available.
